**Formative Assessment 7: Campus-Related Statistical Analysis**

**Part 1: Campus-Related Issues Using Exponential Distribution**

**Scenario**

The selected campus-related problem is the waiting time between printing
services at printing services located at the 2nd floor library. Rather than
measuring the time between customers arriving, the observation focused on
the time interval between one printing service being completed and the next
printing service being completed.

The exponential distribution was selected because it can be used to model
waiting times between events that occur randomly over time.

**Data Collection**

I, as an observer, quietly settled near the printing area from 14:09 to 15:08
(2:09pm - 3:08pm) on October 1. A clock app from my phone was used for
stopwatch, recording the duration between completed printing services. By the
end of observing, a total of 35 data were collected. The observations were
recorded in seconds using Excel and were later analyzed using R.

The observations represent intervals between printing services rather than
individual customer arrival times.

The mean waiting time was calculated from the 35 recorded intervals. The
rate parameter, lambda, was then estimated as the reciprocal of the
mean waiting time.

The exponential probability density function (PDF) and cumulative
distribution function (CDF) were also calculated using R. In addition,
the probabilities of a printing service occurring within one, two, and
five minutes were determined.

**Results**

The analysis produced the following results:

Number of observations: 35

Mean waiting time: 100.4829 seconds

Mean waiting time: 1.6747 minutes

Standard deviation: 103.3149 seconds

Lambda per second: 0.009952

Lambda per minute: 0.597117

Expected waiting time: 100.4829 seconds

Expected waiting time: 1.6747 minutes
 

The calculated probabilities were:
 
Within 1 minute: 44.96%

Within 2 minutes: 69.71%

Within 5 minutes: 94.95%


The coefficient of variation was 1.0282. This is close to 1, which is
consistent with an important characteristic of the exponential
distribution, where the theoretical coefficient of variation is 1.

![Histogram with Exponential PDF]("D:\r fas\fa7\Part1 ggplot.jpg")

![Q-Q Plot for Exponential Distribution]("D:\r fas\fa7\Part1 qqplot.jpg")

**Interpretation**

The results indicate that the average interval between completed printing
services was approximately 100.48 seconds, or 1.67 minutes. Based on the
fitted exponential model, there is a 44.96% probability that another
printing service will be completed within one minute. This probability
increases to 69.71% within two minutes and 94.95% within five minutes.

These results suggest that although printing services generally occur
within a relatively short interval, the actual waiting time can vary
considerably. The standard deviation of 103.31 seconds is close to the
mean waiting time, which is consistent with the variability expected from
an exponential waiting-time model.

The histogram shows that most printing service intervals were short, while
only a few took much longer. The data are right-skewed, which is a common
shape for an exponential distribution. The exponential curve generally follows
the pattern of the observed data, so the model provides a reasonable
approximation of the waiting times.

The Q-Q plot shows that most of the observed values are reasonably close to
the reference line, especially for the smaller and middle waiting times.
However, the larger waiting times deviate from the line, with the longest
interval being noticeably higher than the theoretical value. This means the
exponential model is a reasonable approximation, but it does not perfectly fit
the extreme observations.

In practical terms, the results can provide a general estimate of how
frequently printing services are completed at the library. This may help
students form reasonable expectations about the time between completed
printing jobs. However, the results should be interpreted as an estimate
based on the observed period and may not represent all operating periods
of the library.



**Part 2. Applying Normal Distribution on Campus**

**Scenario**

The selected variable is the amount of time people spent in Freedom Park. The
purpose of this observation was to examine how long people typically remained
in the area and determine whether the observed data followed a pattern that
could reasonably be described using a normal distribution.

**Data Collection**

Observations were conducted in the Freedom Park, a popular spot among the
students, on October 1 from 15:19 to 16:56 (3:19pm - 4:56pm). I keep track of
the records using Samsung Notes on my phone. Data include the number of people
observed, their starting time to stay in that area, and the time they left.
These were input in Excel to compute for the total minutes people spent.

The observation was conducted without directly interacting with or
disturbing the people. I quietly recorded the necessary information without
intentionally focusing attention on individuals.

A total of 53 people were represented in the dataset. When multiple
people had the same recorded duration, the frequency was retained in the
analysis so that each person contributed to the statistical calculations.

The frequency of each recorded duration was organized into a frequency
distribution table. The mean, standard deviation, and median were then
calculated.

The mean time spent was used as mu, while the standard deviation was
used as sigma. The observed data were also compared with the
theoretical normal distribution.

The percentage of observations within one, two, and three standard
deviations of the mean was calculated. An interquartile range (IQR)
method was also used to identify potential outliers.

**Results**

The analysis produced the following descriptive statistics:

Number of people: 53

Mean time spent: 16.8868 minutes

Standard deviation: 16.6001 minutes

Median: 11 minutes

Minimum: 1 minute

Maximum: 60 minutes

 
Frequency Distribution Table

```{r}

part2 <- read.csv("D:/r fas/fa7/data2.csv")
part2 <- part2[1:38, 1:4]
totalp <- sum(part2$PEOPLE)

duration_data <- rep(
  part2$MINUTES_SPENT,
  part2$PEOPLE
)

frequency_table <- as.data.frame(table(duration_data))

names(frequency_table) <- c(
  "MINUTES_SPENT",
  "FREQUENCY"
)

frequency_table$MINUTES_SPENT <-
  as.numeric(as.character(frequency_table$MINUTES_SPENT))

frequency_table$PERCENTAGE <-
  frequency_table$FREQUENCY / totalp * 100

print(frequency_table)

```

The percentage of observations within each standard-deviation range was:

Within 1sd: 83.02%

Within 2sd: 92.45%

Within 3sd: 100.00%


For comparison, the theoretical percentages for a perfectly normal
distribution are approximately 68.27%, 95.45%, and 99.73% within one,
two, and three standard deviations, respectively.

![Histogram with Normal Distribution Curve]("D:\r fas\fa7\Part2 ggplot.jpg")

![Box Plot]("D:\r fas\fa7\Part2 boxplot.jpg")

**Distribution Shape and Symmetry**

The distribution is not symmetric and is likely right-skewed. The mean
of 16.89 minutes is greater than the median of 11 minutes. This difference
suggests that the longer durations pull the mean toward the right side of
the distribution.

The observed data also contain several relatively long stays compared
with the more frequent shorter stays. Therefore, the data do not appear
to follow a perfectly normal distribution.

**Outliers**

Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, the first quartile (Q1) was 5 minutes and the
third quartile (Q3) was 25 minutes. The IQR was therefore 20 minutes.

The lower and upper bounds were calculated as -25 minutes and 55 minutes,
respectively. Three observations were identified as outliers, all having
a duration of 60 minutes.

These observations indicate that a small number of people remained in the
park substantially longer than most of the observed individuals.

**Interpretation and Usefulness**

The results show that people spent an average of approximately 16.89
minutes in the campus park, although the relatively large standard
deviation of 16.60 minutes indicates considerable variation in the amount
of time spent there.

The right-skewed shape suggests that shorter visits were more common,
while a smaller number of people stayed for considerably longer periods.
The three 60-minute observations contribute to the longer right tail of
the distribution.

The histogram indicates that time spent in Freedom Park is not normally
distributed. Most individuals spent relatively short periods in the park,
while a smaller number stayed considerably longer. The distribution is
positively (right) skewed, with values extending to approximately 60 minutes.
The normal distribution curve does not closely match the observed data.

The box plot shows that the median time spent in Freedom Park was approximately
10–11 minutes. The middle 50% of observations were roughly between 5 and 25
minutes. The distribution is positively skewed, with a long upper tail. There
is also an apparent high-value outlier at approximately 60 minutes, indicating
that one observation involved a substantially longer stay than most visitors.

The data may be useful for understanding how students and other campus
users utilize the park. For example, the information could help provide
an estimate of typical visit duration and could contribute to decisions
regarding seating, space allocation, or other improvements to the area.
However, because the observations were collected during a particular
observation period, the results should not be assumed to represent every
person who uses the campus park at all times.



**Summary and Conclusion**

The two parts demonstrate how probability distributions can be applied
to campus-related observations. The printing-service data produced an
average interval of approximately 1.67 minutes between completed services,
with the exponential model estimating a 94.95% probability of another
service occurring within five minutes. The campus-park data showed an
average stay of approximately 16.89 minutes and a right-skewed
distribution rather than a perfectly symmetric normal distribution.

Overall, the analysis demonstrates how collected campus observations can
be summarized and interpreted using probability and statistical methods.
